title: System Script Proxy Execution: PubPrn
summary: PubPrn is a specific instance of the parent technique: a signed Visual Basic script that ships with Windows to publish printers into Active Directory Domain Services, normally launched through the command line script host. The script takes a printer and a destination, and its second parameter accepts a scriptlet moniker, which allowed a remote scriptlet file to be pulled over HTTP or HTTPS and executed in the context of the trusted script. That combination made it useful for defence evasion, because a permitted signed script performed both the download and the execution, and application control that trusted the script did not inspect the remote content. Later versions of Windows restrict the second parameter to the directory protocol, so the remote scriptlet path no longer works on current builds. Detection focuses on process creation for the script host: the script name in the command line, a scriptlet or web address where a directory path belongs, and the network connection or child process that follows. Legitimate use publishes a printer with a directory container path.

beginner.definition: PubPrn is a small Microsoft script that comes with Windows and is used to publish printers. This sub-technique means an attacker abuses that script to run a file from the internet. It is one named example of the parent idea. It differs from the parent because it names one exact script and one exact trick.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers prefer tools that already exist on the computer. PubPrn is signed, so security tools often allow it to run. In the past its second setting also accepted a web address, which let it fetch remote code. That let an attacker run code while bypassing many controls. Later versions of Windows block the trick, but older systems may still be at risk.
howItWorks: The parent technique covers trusted scripts in general; this one names PubPrn.
PubPrn normally publishes a printer into a directory container such as Active Directory.
It runs through the command line script host and accepts two arguments.
Attackers found that the second argument also accepted a remote scriptlet address.
The trusted script then downloaded and ran the scriptlet, which carried the payload.
Later Windows versions limit that argument to the directory protocol, blocking the trick.
beginner.example: Imagine a council office where one clerk has a signed form for booking printers into the registry. The form has two boxes: which printer, and where to record it. Somebody notices that the second box also accepts a note saying bring a parcel from an outside address. The clerk, simply following the form, fetches the parcel and opens it. Later the council changes the form so only registry addresses are accepted.
takeaways: One signed Windows script was abused to run remote code through a trusted process.
Watch the second argument of printer publishing commands, not only the script name.
Later Windows versions limit this trick, so patch and retire old systems.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique relates to the parent proxy execution technique.
Describe what PubPrn does in normal administrative use.
Explain how a scriptlet argument allowed remote code to run through the script.
Identify the process creation details that reveal abuse of this script.
Explain why later Windows versions reduce the risk of this behaviour.
